Press enter or click to view image in full size Product teams have never had more technology. We have analytics platforms telling us what users are doing. Research repositories telling us what customers are saying. Roadmapping tools showing what we intend to build. Delivery tools showing what teams are building. And AI assistants helping us write, summarize, analyze, and generate. And yet, something still feels fundamentally disconnected. A customer signal appears in one system. Research happens somewhere else. A decision gets captured in a meeting, document, or slide. Delivery moves into another tool. The feature launches. Analytics tells us what happened. Then, three months later, somebody asks: Why did we make that decision? Or: Did it actually work? Or perhaps the most important question: What did we learn that should change the next decision? Too often, answering those questions means reconstructing the story manually. I think this is one of the next problems AI needs to solve in product management. Not another assistant. An AI-native Product Operating System. The first wave of AI made individual tasks faster Much of the first wave of AI in product management has focused on productivity. Write a PRD. Summarize hundreds of pieces of feedback. Generate user stories. Analyze an interview. Create a roadmap. Draft a strategy. Prepare a stakeholder update. These are useful capabilities. I use many of them myself. But they mostly optimize individual steps in an existing process. We are putting increasingly powerful AI into a product operating model that was largely designed before this level of AI existed. And that creates an interesting problem. In addition to disconnected product tools, we can now have disconnected AI conversations, generated artifacts, agents, and recommendations. So I’ve become increasingly interested in a different question: What would product management look like if the operating model itself were designed around intelligence? The Connected Intelligence Loop I’ve been experimenting with this idea around a simple lifecycle: Signal → Evidence → Research → Opportunity → Assumptions → Decision → Design → Delivery → Outcome → Learning → Memory Press enter or click to view image in full size The important part isn’t the number of stages. It’s the connection between them. A signal shouldn’t disappear after discovery. Research shouldn’t become a forgotten document. A decision shouldn’t lose the evidence that supported it. Delivery shouldn’t lose the reason the work exists. Measurement shouldn’t be disconnected from the prediction we originally made. And learning shouldn’t disappear into another retrospective. Each stage should make the next one smarter. And eventually, the end of the process should improve the beginning of the next one. That’s the loop. Imagine a different product workflow Suppose engagement among a group of users suddenly drops by 7%. Normally, a Product Manager might need to open several tools. Check analytics. Ask for cohort analysis. Search customer feedback. Look at recent releases. Check delivery activity. Speak to Design. Review previous research. Then begin forming a hypothesis. But imagine an intelligence layer capable of connecting that context. It might start with: What changed? Engagement declined by 7%. Then continue: Which users? The decline is concentrated in a particular new-user cohort. Where in their journey? The largest behavioral drop occurs between two important activation steps. What are customers saying? Recent feedback contains increasing references to friction around the same part of the experience. What changed recently? Two releases affected that journey during the same period. And then something particularly interesting: Have we seen this before? A previous initiative addressed a similar behavioral pattern. What happened then? The intervention improved the target behavior — but by considerably less than the team originally predicted. Now we’re no longer asking AI merely to summarize information. We’re asking it to build decision context . Product management is a decision-making function This distinction matters. Product management ultimately isn’t a document-production function. It is a decision-making function under uncertainty. Which means the most valuable AI systems for product teams shouldn’t ultimately be measured by how many documents they generate.
